newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Mekong floods boost Vietnamese rice prices - trade.
newsitem.headline: Mekong floods boost Vietnamese rice prices - trade.

text.p: Extensive flooding in the Mekong delta has caused supply bottlenecks in the Vietnamese rice market and underpinned both domestic and export prices, traders said on Thursday.
Five percent broken rice was quoted at around US$275-$285 a tonne FOB Saigon port compared with $275-$280 a week ago. Ten percent grade was around $5-$10 per tonne lower.
"Prices...seem to be moving up because of doubts about damage in the Mekong delta," said one trader in Bangkok. "And levels of rice coming into Saigon port seem to be low because of the flooding."

Relief workers in the country's main rice-growing area said last week that 46,513 hectares (114,930 acres) of the delta's paddy fields were under water, more than six percent of which had been completely destroyed.
However, traders in Ho Chi Minh City said that with just an estimated 1.5 percent of the summer-autumn crop left to be harvested, there had been very little damage to paddy.
"The rice is there in the delta, that's not the problem," said one. "It's transport and milling delays that are making it tough for exporters."
Traders said demand from abroad remained buoyant, with five vessels bound for Iran now loading in Saigon Port.

The official daily Nhan Dan reported that measures were being put in place to help traders buy 230,000 tonnes of rice from areas affected by flooding to support local farmers, many of whose storehouses have been washed away or damaged.
It said banks had been instructed to offer rice buyers preferential loan rates and the Finance Ministry was considering an export tax holiday for traders during the last three months of the year.
Faced with a balloning trade deficit, the government earlier this month raised its export quota for rice to 3.0 million tonnes from 2.5 million.
Vietnam sold 2.025 million tonnes of rice to overseas buyers in 1995, making it the world's fourth-largest exporter of the grain after the United States, Thailand and India.
